problem: Jalisco's tequila industry leaves behind about 915,000 tonnes of agave bagasse a year, the fibre left after the sugars are extracted (Warren-Vega et al., 2025), in line with the 2.18 million tonnes of agave processed in 2025 (CNIT). Most of it is burned, dumped or left in open piles to rot. Distilleries treat it as a cost: the general coordinator of a distillery I interviewed pays 200 to 500 pesos per tonne to haul it away, and a compost operator told me there are no authorized disposal sites. The people exposed live in the rural towns of the agave region, where the tequila chain sustains more than 100,000 jobs (CNIT): burning releases carbon dioxide, black carbon and particulates, and open piles release methane and leachates and shelter flies, pests and rodents. Globally, open biomass burning, crop residues included, produces about 37 percent of black carbon emissions (Bond et al., 2013), and Latin America repeats the pattern with sugarcane bagasse, coffee residues and corn stover. Meanwhile, a restaurant supplier in my network reports that gourmet mushrooms such as shiitake and lion's mane often come from other states or are imported.
serve: Three groups. First, distilleries and agave growers. Bagasse costs them money and space, and they are underserved because their only routes are burning, dumping or low-value compost: one distillery coordinator I interviewed pays 200 to 500 pesos per tonne for hauling. Fungi Mati turns that cost into a supply relationship, starting with distilleries, whose residue is concentrated, since field growers did not answer my outreach. Their rural neighbours benefit too: a woman living a kilometre from a distillery has grown used to the smell and flies, so the change is fewer fires and rotting piles near homes. Second, restaurants and households in Guadalajara and nearby areas, served today by gourmet mushrooms that often travel from other states or are imported. They get fresh mushrooms grown locally, through a restaurant distributor and a well-connected saleswoman in my network and a 700-member gourmet food community. Third, people who want to learn to grow without a lab: my 2026 PrepaTec pilot reached 85 students, teachers, staff and visitors, I helped teach a course for 50 young women in January, and I sell grow kits and courses built around a pressure cooker and a plastic tent.
innovative: Most mushroom farms in Mexico grow on straw or sawdust pellets, some of them imported, and treat the substrate as a commodity. Fungi Mati starts from the opposite end: the region's most abundant residue, agave bagasse, which today is burned, dumped or composted slowly, becomes gourmet mushrooms in four to six weeks. That speed is the core of the solution. In the time compost takes to half-break down, the same fibre has already become food that sells by the kilogram, and the spent substrate still returns to the soil. Pelletized bagasse makes it repeatable: pellets standardize moisture and particle size, store for months and cost about half of a conventional substrate, at 22,000 to 24,000 pesos per tonne. Of the ten existing bagasse uses I benchmarked, from adobe bricks and briquettes to bioplastics and compost, none turns it into a high-value food through a model a small producer can run. The approach is already shifting the local market: after our conversations, my pellet supplier began producing a mushroom-specific bagasse pellet mix in October 2026, a product any grower can now buy. Because it needs no industrial plant, it can be copied by a grower in any town near a distillery, and knowledge travels with it through courses, kits and an AI tutor built with guidance and early support from Equitech Futures. If enough growers adopt it, bagasse stops being a disposal cost and becomes a traded input that distilleries can sell. As an exploratory line, at the Carrillo Biorefinery Lab with Dr. Danay Carrillo Nieves, I will test whether crossing single-spore monokaryons of two Pleurotus parental strains yields a strain better adapted to bagasse; if it works, the method travels to spent coffee grounds, corn stover or sugarcane bagasse.
impact: Inputs: pelletized agave bagasse from a local pelletizer, Pleurotus strains from the lab collection, low-cost sterile and fruiting equipment, and my cultivation protocol. Activities: pasteurize and inoculate substrate, grow and harvest, sell fresh mushrooms and kits, teach courses with and without the AI tutor, and breed strains for bagasse. Outputs in year one: one tonne of bagasse diverted from burning or dumping, at least 600 kilograms of gourmet mushrooms sold to Guadalajara restaurants and a 700-member gourmet community, the first strains screened on bagasse, and at least two courses. Short-term outcomes: restaurants get fresh mushrooms grown a few kilometres away instead of produce brought from other states or imported; course participants can grow at home with a pressure cooker and a plastic tent. Medium-term: a disposal cost for one distillery becomes a supply contract. Long-term: an open protocol and strain set that growers across Latin America can apply to their own residues, and less bagasse burned or dumped per tonne processed. Evidence for each link: distilleries already pay 200 to 500 pesos per tonne to get rid of bagasse (interview), so supply is available and motivated; Pleurotus reaches 41 to 66 percent biological efficiency on agave bagasse (Lagunes-Reyes et al., 2023), and my own triplicate bags reached about 50 percent over two weighed flushes; the PrepaTec pilot, on sawdust pellets, showed the system works outside a lab, with 85 people reached; and kit and course sales show willingness to pay. The main assumption to test is steady restaurant demand at that volume. I will track kilograms of bagasse processed and harvested, biological efficiency per strain, revenue per channel and people trained, disaggregated by sex, in a monthly log.
team: Full-time staff: none. Part-time: one, me, the founder and team lead, working on Fungi Mati alongside my biotechnology engineering degree. Contractors: none yet; the first hire, once production is steady, would be a part-time grower. Unpaid support: my academic mentor, Dr. Danay Carrillo Nieves (Carrillo Biorefinery Lab); my father, who provides the house where the farm is being set up; about 20 B-Eco student volunteers at Tec de Monterrey for outreach and field work; and an outreach collaborator, science communicator Dora González Parra.
why: The biology works; what I lack is the structure to grow it responsibly. Four barriers. Market: reaching distilleries, jimadores and restaurant buyers directly has been the hardest part of this project, and intermediaries have not worked; introductions through Solve's network of companies, foundations and food-system organizations, including the tequila industry, would turn disposal costs into supply contracts and secure steady buyers. Technical: I need a rigorous way to measure impact, tonnes of bagasse diverted, emissions avoided, food produced and people trained, and, as a bagasse researcher urged me, public-health effects, so that funders and buyers can trust the numbers; Solve's monitoring and evaluation support fits that need. Legal: Fungi Mati is not yet registered, and selling food to restaurants requires formalizing the business and meeting food-safety rules; Solve's legal and business partners could guide that step. Know-how: as a solo founder, I want mentorship and conversations with past Solvers who have taken a bio-based product from one pilot to many. Solve's support would also help make the method transferable to other residues across Latin America.
